You judge a requirements contract. A model interviewed the future users of a service and derived a contract from what they told it. You compare that contract with the reference requirements of the same service.

=== REFERENCE REQUIREMENTS (read-only) ===
BR-01: The service serves several independent operating companies at once. The staff of one operating company can never see or change another operating company's drones, models, sites, charging pads, jobs or flights, or their history.

BR-02: The airspace picture (the corridors between sites, the zones that group them, the prohibited zones and the closures) is one and the same for every company, and every company's staff can see all of it.

BR-03: Every member of staff acts in one of three roles: fleet technician or dispatcher at an operating company, or the airspace desk at the platform company. Each action of the service can be taken only by the role these requirements give it to.

BR-04: The airspace desk cannot see any one company's drones, jobs or flights.

BR-05: A fleet technician can add a drone to their company's fleet, stating its model. For each model the service holds how much it can carry, how far it can fly on a full battery, which sensors it carries, and which charging connector it uses.

BR-06: Each drone has a home site, one of its company's sites.

BR-07: A fleet technician can retire a drone. A retired drone stays in its company's history and is never again given a flight or sent to charge.

BR-08: A fleet technician can take a drone out of service for repair and put it back into service. A drone out of service cannot be given a flight.

BR-09: A fleet technician can set up a charging pad at one of their company's sites, stating its connector type.

BR-10: A charging pad is used only by drones of the company that owns it.

BR-11: A fleet technician can send a drone to charge. The service sends it only to a pad whose connector type is the one the drone's model uses, and refuses otherwise.

BR-12: The service keeps, for each drone, a record of when it was taken out of service, repaired or serviced, and put back, and by whom, so that its company can show a regulator how the drone has been looked after.

BR-13: A dispatcher can record a delivery job: a load to be carried from one site to another.

BR-14: A dispatcher can record an inspection job: the sensors it needs and a list of points to visit in a set order, ending back where it started.

BR-15: A dispatcher plans a flight for a job by choosing the drone and the way, a chain of corridors between named sites.

BR-16: The service never chooses a drone or a way for a flight, and never puts one in place of the dispatcher's choice.

BR-17: On a dispatcher's request, the service shows which of their company's drones could get to where a job starts.

BR-18: A flight leaves only after a dispatcher has signed it off; nothing but a dispatcher's own action signs a flight off.

BR-19: A dispatcher can call off a flight.

BR-20: The service refuses to sign off a flight whose drone cannot do the job: a load heavier than its model can carry, a way longer than its model can fly, or, for an inspection, a sensor the job needs that its model does not carry.

BR-21: The service refuses to sign off a flight whose way passes through a zone where flying is prohibited, or through a closure in force at any time during the flight.

BR-22: The service does not let more drones take off or land at a site at the same time than the site has places for.

BR-23: When dispatchers planning at the same time sign off flights that would use the same drone at overlapping times, only one sign-off succeeds, and the others are told why they failed.

BR-24: When it judges whether a drone can fly a way, the service does not count on the full range of a full battery, since batteries drain faster in cold and wind than planned.

BR-25: The service accepts reports from people and devices outside the company that a flight's load is ready, that its drone has reached a point of its job, and that it has arrived, and it records each against the flight.

BR-26: A report that arrives more than once is applied once.

BR-27: A report that arrives late or out of order never undoes a later one: a flight's state follows the order in which things happened, not the order in which the reports arrived.

BR-28: When a report a flight is waiting for does not come in time, such as its arrival, the service flags the flight to the dispatchers of its company, since nobody watches every drone.

BR-29: A drone that restarts in flight and carries on stays on the same flight, and its reports after the restart count for that flight.

BR-30: The airspace desk can record the corridors between named sites, the zones that group them, and the zones where the authorities prohibit flying.

BR-31: The airspace desk can enter a planned closure, with a start and an end time, and a sudden closure, which applies at once. It can amend a closure, for example by widening its area or moving its end time, and the amendment applies from the moment it is entered.

BR-32: When a closure is entered or amended, the service tells each company's dispatchers which of their flights it affects, including flights already in the air, and tells no company about another's flights.

BR-33: The service does not itself call off, reroute or change a flight because of a closure; that is the dispatcher's decision.

BR-34: When a closure is entered, the airspace desk sees how much disruption it caused across the customers, as totals that name no company and show no company's flights.

BR-35: The service can be restarted, or crash, while drones are flying, and afterwards carries on from where it was: nothing it had recorded is lost or applied twice.

BR-36: An instruction the service sends to a drone or to charging equipment takes effect once, even when it gets through twice or the service sends it again because it cannot tell whether the first attempt arrived.

BR-37: The service tells each company's own systems what happens to that company's drones and jobs, and nothing about any other company's.

BR-38: The service offers no way to steer a drone.
=== END OF REFERENCE REQUIREMENTS ===

The names in the reference that look like `name` stand for these values:
(none)

=== OUT OF SCOPE: things the users said they do not want ===
- Management or analytical reports, exports, and dashboards.
- Login through an external identity provider.
- i18n.
- Compliance with any regulation, or a compliance audit. Regulations are cited as provenance only (`domain-profile.md` §9).
- Data retention and erasure: no retention schedule, deletion on request, or pseudonymisation of history.
- Backups.
- High availability or multi-node deployment.
- User accounts, sign-up, passwords, or user management. Staff identities are issued outside the system; each request carries a signed token (D-23).
- Notifying people by e-mail, text message, or phone. Domain events go only to the event webhook (D-18).
- Route planning or automatic choice of a drone. The system validates the dispatcher's choice and never makes it (D-33).
- Remote piloting or real-time flight control. Flight control is on the drone (`domain-profile.md` §2).
- Weather data or forecasts.
- Billing, invoicing, or pricing of deliveries and inspections.
- Onboarding of new operating companies or management of tenants through the system.
=== TECHNICAL ADDITIONS: never stated by the users, and not counted against a contract ===
- Autoscaling.
- A second-level cache.
- A message broker, queue, or coordinator. Every boundary is HTTP (`domain-profile.md` §3).
- Geometric or geospatial computation. Position is a location or a corridor; coordinates, if present, are descriptive (`domain-profile.md` §4, §6).
- Throughput or latency at the declared scale. Scale is data context (`domain-profile.md` §7); the harness does not apply fleet-scale load during functional gates.
=== END OF LISTS ===

You receive the contract: a list of items, each with an id and a requirement.

For each reference requirement, decide how the contract as a whole covers it:

- covered: the items, together, state every obligation of the requirement — every rule, condition, exception, value and outcome it gives. Wording, order, the words chosen for states and roles, and whether a value is given by its name or by its number do not matter; meaning does.
- partial: the items state at least one of its obligations and leave out at least one other.
- missing: no item states any of its obligations.

An item states an obligation only when it says what the service must do, or must not do, in a case the requirement covers. A general wish, such as that the service be reliable, states none. An item that says the opposite of an obligation does not state it. A requirement that only names another one, or a value another one defines, does not take over that other requirement's obligations.

For each item of the contract, decide its class:

- reference: it states one or more obligations of the reference requirements; name each requirement it states obligations of.
- user_visible: it asks for something on the out-of-scope list.
- technical: it asks for something on the list of technical additions.
- other: none of these — it asks for something no reference requirement asks for, or states nothing checkable.

A contract with no items covers nothing.

Reply with JSON only: an object with two keys. "requirements" is a list with exactly one entry for every reference requirement, in the reference's order; each entry has "id", the requirement's id, "coverage", one of "covered", "partial" or "missing", and "items", the ids of the items that state its obligations (an empty list when it is missing). "items" is a list with exactly one entry for every item of the contract, in the contract's order; each entry has "id", the item's id, "class", one of "reference", "user_visible", "technical" or "other", and "requirements", the ids of the reference requirements it states obligations of (an empty list unless its class is "reference").

The contract has 50 items:

- id: DR-01
  requirement: The service must allow onboarding new customer companies into separate workspaces without disrupting existing customer companies.
- id: DR-02
  requirement: The service must prevent any customer company user from viewing, creating, modifying, or deleting another company's drones, battery packs, sites, charging pads, maintenance records, jobs, routes, or flight logs.
- id: DR-03
  requirement: The service must prevent the airspace desk from viewing customer-identifying business details, including private jobs, payloads, sites, routes, or company-specific operational problems, except non-identifying aggregate impact or authorized compliance summaries.
- id: DR-04
  requirement: The service must prevent customer company users from creating, editing, or deleting shared airspace restrictions or advisories.
- id: DR-05
  requirement: The service must restrict actions within a company by assigned role—fleet technician or dispatcher—while allowing a single user to hold both roles for their own company if assigned.
- id: DR-06
  requirement: The service must prevent a dispatcher whose dispatcher license is missing, expired, or suspended from signing off flights, acknowledging warnings, issuing in-flight commands, or accepting flight handovers.
- id: DR-07
  requirement: The service must allow a fleet technician to register company operating sites with coordinates, altitude, operating hours, and landing or pad capacity.
- id: DR-08
  requirement: The service must allow a fleet technician to set up charging pads at a company site with a pad identifier, compatible drone models or connectors, maximum power output, and operational status.
- id: DR-09
  requirement: The service must enforce that each charging pad holds at most one drone at a time.
- id: DR-10
  requirement: The service must allow a fleet technician to take a charging pad out of service or return it to service, and must prevent assigning or sending drones to pads that are occupied, incompatible, faulted, or out of service.
- id: DR-11
  requirement: The service must allow a fleet technician to register a drone with a registration unique within the company's fleet, serial number, model, weight and payload limits, battery capacity or compatible packs, cruise speed, maximum range, home site, installed equipment, and approvals for flight over people or in bad weather.
- id: DR-12
  requirement: The service must mark every newly registered drone as unavailable for dispatch until a fleet technician records a passed initial inspection and marks it ready.
- id: DR-13
  requirement: The service must track fixed and swappable battery packs with pack identifier, cycle count, health percentage, and state of charge, recording which pack is installed in each drone and blocking installation or use of retired or damaged packs.
- id: DR-14
  requirement: The service must track each drone's cumulative flight hours, flight cycles, and battery charge cycles against configured hour or calendar maintenance intervals and scheduled maintenance windows.
- id: DR-15
  requirement: The service must flag a drone as due for inspection and block new flight sign-offs whenever it reaches a maintenance threshold, reports an in-flight fault such as a hard landing, battery fault, or sensor warning, or makes an unexpected off-destination landing, until a fleet technician clears the inspection.
- id: DR-16
  requirement: The service must allow a fleet technician to take an idle drone out of service for repair by recording a reason, log repair work and replaced parts, and block returning the drone to service until the repair is closed and an inspection passes.
- id: DR-17
  requirement: The service must prevent taking a drone out of service while it is actively in flight, and when a drone assigned to an upcoming signed-off flight is taken out of service, must alert the responsible dispatcher and block departure.
- id: DR-18
  requirement: The service must allow a fleet technician to retire a drone with a retirement date and reason, permanently preventing it from being assigned to flights or returned to service while retaining all of its historical records.
- id: DR-19
  requirement: The service must provide technicians and dispatchers with a company-scoped readiness view showing each drone's current status—available, charging, reserved, in flight, due for maintenance, out of service, or retired—and charging pad availability at each site.
- id: DR-20
  requirement: The service must allow a fleet technician to send a drone to charge on an available, compatible charging pad at its current site, and must block the request if the pad is busy, incompatible, faulted, or out of service.
- id: DR-21
  requirement: The service must prevent a drone from being launched while still connected to a charging pad or assigned to a flight starting before its battery is projected to reach the required charge.
- id: DR-22
  requirement: The service must update a charging drone's battery level from incoming telemetry, and if the charging pad faults or disconnects during a session, must alert technicians and affected dispatchers, mark the session interrupted or unknown rather than complete, and prevent clearing the drone as charged until telemetry confirms actual charge and pad release.
- id: DR-23
  requirement: The service must ensure that duplicate deliveries of any drone or charging pad command—including launch, hold, return to home, divert, abort, start charging, or release—are executed at most once.
- id: DR-24
  requirement: The service must track and display the delivery status of every command sent to a drone or charging pad as pending, acknowledged, failed, or timed out with unknown outcome, rather than assuming delivery succeeded.
- id: DR-25
  requirement: The service must allow the airspace desk to create shared airspace restrictions and weather advisories specifying polygon or circle geometry, altitude floor and ceiling with explicit height reference, UTC start and end timestamps with local display, issuing authority, reference number, reason, and severity as either advisory warning or hard flight block.
- id: DR-26
  requirement: The service must reject publishing any airspace restriction or advisory that has missing authority details, invalid geometry such as a self-intersecting polygon or zero radius, or an end time earlier than its start time.
- id: DR-27
  requirement: The service must support immediate or future scheduled activation of airspace restrictions and allow the airspace desk to update, extend, shrink, or cancel a restriction early while preserving full change history and archiving expired or cancelled entries.
- id: DR-28
  requirement: The service must prevent silent overwrites when multiple airspace desk operators edit the same restriction concurrently by rejecting stale updates and presenting the current version.
- id: DR-29
  requirement: When active airspace restrictions overlap in space and time, the service must enforce the strictest rule, such that a hard flight block overrides an advisory warning and the lowest altitude ceiling governs.
- id: DR-30
  requirement: The service must allow the airspace desk to record an authority-issued exemption against a restriction for a specific company, flight, or waiver reference with its validity window and issuing authority, and must keep that exemption invisible to all other companies.
- id: DR-31
  requirement: When a shared airspace restriction or advisory is published, updated, or cancelled, the service must apply the change immediately to flight checks, re-evaluate all companies' planned, signed-off, and active flights, and immediately alert affected dispatchers.
- id: DR-32
  requirement: The service must allow dispatchers to manage company-private missions—such as parcel deliveries, multi-waypoint infrastructure inspections, or urgent hospital logistics—with priority, time windows, payload weight, required equipment or sensors, and delivery or chain-of-custody confirmation requirements.
- id: DR-33
  requirement: The service must allow dispatchers to plan a flight route specifying departure site, waypoints including hover or loiter intervals, cruising altitude, destination or return site, and scheduled departure and arrival times.
- id: DR-34
  requirement: The service must warn dispatchers while drafting a flight plan if another draft plan already references the same drone or overlapping site or charging pad slot.
- id: DR-35
  requirement: Before allowing flight sign-off, the service must verify that the assigned drone is ready for dispatch, has no open faults or overlapping scheduled or predicted maintenance, meets payload weight, required equipment, and over-people or bad-weather approvals, and operates within site opening hours.
- id: DR-36
  requirement: Before allowing flight sign-off, the service must verify that the drone's installed battery state of charge and current health provide sufficient range for the full planned route—including altitude changes, loiter or hover time, known weather margin, and mandatory reserve—and block sign-off if insufficient.
- id: DR-37
  requirement: Before allowing flight sign-off, the service must verify that the route and time window do not violate any active or scheduled hard-block airspace restriction unless a valid company exemption applies, and must require explicit dispatcher acknowledgment of any overlapping advisory warnings.
- id: DR-38
  requirement: The service must support prioritizing urgent missions, such as hospital logistics, in dispatch queues and allowing authorized preemption of unlaunched lower-priority flights for drone or site reservations.
- id: DR-39
  requirement: At flight sign-off, the service must atomically lock the assigned drone and required site and charging pad slots including turnaround buffers so concurrent dispatchers cannot double-book them, rejecting any conflicting sign-off with a clear reason.
- id: DR-40
  requirement: Upon sign-off, the service must record the dispatcher's identity, active license verification, acknowledged warnings, and timestamp, and track the flight through draft, signed off, in flight, completed, diverted, aborted, and cancelled states.
- id: DR-41
  requirement: Immediately before launch, the service must perform a pre-flight check of drone readiness, battery charge, pad release, absence of faults, and current airspace and weather clearance, blocking takeoff and alerting the dispatcher if any condition fails or a new blocking restriction overlaps a signed-off flight.
- id: DR-42
  requirement: When a signed-off flight is cancelled before takeoff, the service must immediately release its drone, route, site, and charging pad reservations.
- id: DR-43
  requirement: When a flight is called off while in flight, the service must require issuing an abort, hold, or return-to-home command toward a safe landing site.
- id: DR-44
  requirement: During an active flight, the service must ingest and display live telemetry including position, altitude, speed, battery level, and equipment or health alerts.
- id: DR-45
  requirement: When radio contact or telemetry drops out during a flight, the service must distinguish stale or lost telemetry from a confirmed landing, display the last known position and last-contact timestamp, and alert the dispatcher when silence exceeds a configured threshold.
- id: DR-46
  requirement: The service must immediately raise a high-priority alert to the responsible dispatcher if an in-flight drone deviates from its approved route corridor or altitude, enters an active or newly issued restricted area, drops below reserve battery, reports a fault, or is delayed past downstream drone or site reservation buffers.
- id: DR-47
  requirement: If telemetry indicates a drone has landed away from its planned destination, the service must flag the flight as an unexpected landing incident rather than completed and flag the drone as requiring technician inspection before its next flight.
- id: DR-48
  requirement: The service must allow transferring responsibility for signed-off or active flights to another licensed dispatcher within the same company, recording the handover and updated responsible dispatcher in the flight log.
- id: DR-49
  requirement: The service must maintain an immutable, timestamped audit log with user attribution for all fleet, battery, pad, maintenance, airspace, exemption, flight plan, sign-off, handover, command, and mission delivery or handoff events.
- id: DR-50
  requirement: The service must allow authorized audits to reconstruct the exact active airspace restrictions, drone and battery state, and flight authorization state at any past date, time, and location without exposing any company's private data to competitors.
